bp: Smart city policy is not just a matter of choosing better sensors or dashboards. A city decision usually sits inside a negotiation: agencies, residents, vendors, health officials, planners, media actors, and environmental groups argue over what problem matters, which options are possible, and whose evidence counts as legitimate. This literature review asks what happens when big data and AI enter that room. The reviewed work, drawn from Scopus, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect, suggests that large datasets and algorithmic tools do more than support a final decision. They can shape the negotiation before people deliberate, by making some uncertainties visible, some futures seem feasible, and some arguments look more authoritative. The paper therefore serves a governance question: in smart city negotiations, analytical capacity itself can become bargaining power, because the actor who structures the information space may also structure the range of acceptable outcomes.
wh: The hard part is that city negotiations are not clean engineering problems with one shared target. Urban planning, environmental governance, health policy, media studies, behavioral science, organizational studies, and computer science each treat evidence, legitimacy, and public value differently. A traffic dataset may make one option look efficient, while residents may worry about surveillance or unequal burden. An algorithmic summary may seem neutral, while its choices about what to count can quietly narrow the debate. The abstract says AI and big data redefine uncertainty, feasibility, and legitimacy, which means the tools affect the terms of disagreement, not just the answer. That makes evaluation difficult: a system can improve information flow while also shifting power among negotiating actors. The review must therefore track both decision support and political mediation, including how algorithmic curation influences public discourse and agenda-setting.
naive: A smart beginner might say: collect more city data, run better analysis, and give negotiators a clearer dashboard. If everyone sees the same facts, the better policy should win. That fails because negotiation is not only a shortage of facts. It is also a struggle over which facts matter, which goals deserve priority, and who gets to define a realistic choice. More data can hide assumptions inside technical outputs. AI tools can pre-select options, rank issues, or frame uncertainty in ways that favor actors with stronger analytical capacity. The beginner's approach treats data as a neutral flashlight, while the reviewed literature treats it as part of the bargaining structure.
ap: The paper's central move is to review highly cited work across several fields and organize it around how data and AI change negotiation itself. Instead of asking only whether algorithms make policy decisions more accurate, it asks how they structure the space in which policy actors bargain. The abstract identifies four connected themes: big data structuring negotiation spaces, algorithms influencing public discourse and agenda-setting, AI tools entering decision-making and negotiated outcomes, and human agency persisting under algorithmic mediation. That organization is the contribution visible from the input. It turns scattered studies from urban planning, environmental governance, health policy, media studies, behavioral science, organizational studies, and computer science into one question: when technical systems enter public negotiation, do they merely inform participants, or do they pre-configure what participants can plausibly argue for?
mech: The mechanism is a literature-review pipeline, not a deployed prediction system. The input is a body of highly cited studies indexed in Scopus, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect. The review reads those studies across multiple disciplines and looks for repeated ways in which large-scale datasets, algorithmic tools, and AI systems appear in policy design and negotiation processes. First, it gathers evidence about where these tools are used, such as urban planning, environmental governance, health policy, and public discourse. Second, it groups the evidence by the role the technology plays: does it define the negotiation space, curate information for the public, help produce decisions, or mediate action while humans remain involved? Third, it compares those roles against negotiation concepts such as uncertainty, feasibility, legitimacy, and bargaining power. The transformed output is not a numerical prediction but a conceptual map of how data systems change the negotiation environment. What gets scored informally is influence: whether a tool only supplies evidence after choices are open, or whether it shapes the menu of choices before deliberation starts. The paper then reports that analytical capacity can function as structural bargaining power.
math: The main mathematical idea is not a new formula in the abstract; it is the logic of information structuring. Large datasets turn scattered city observations into counted categories, trends, and comparisons. That is a compression step: many individual events become a smaller set of measures that negotiators can discuss. Algorithmic curation adds ranking and selection: among many possible facts, reports, voices, and issues, some are placed in front of decision-makers or the public while others recede. AI-assisted decision-making adds prediction or scenario comparison: different policy options can be made to look more or less feasible depending on what the system treats as evidence and what goal it is set to favor. The important tradeoff is clarity versus control. Mathematical ordering and summarizing can reduce confusion, but they also decide which differences are ignored. Probability enters when uncertainty is redefined as an estimated chance rather than an open political concern. Ranking enters when agendas are shaped by selected information. These ideas fit because negotiation depends on shared representations; whoever controls the representation can affect the bargain before choices appear fully public.
dots: This paper connects to several recurring conference ideas, but through governance rather than model performance. It sits near ranking because public agenda-setting often means deciding which issues, facts, and options rise to attention. It sits near probability because smart city policy must act under uncertain futures in health, environment, planning, and public behavior. It sits near causality because policy actors need to know whether an intervention would actually change an outcome, not just whether variables move together in city data. It also connects to fairness and responsible AI because the abstract says algorithmic mediation can alter power relations among negotiating actors. Neighboring papers in the same batch study recommendation agents, advertising bidding, agentic e-commerce, security inspection, and fair allocation; all involve systems that do not merely process information but change the choices available to humans. This review applies that same pressure to public policy negotiation.
ww: The review works, if it works, because it refuses to separate technical capacity from negotiation power. A plain technology-adoption review might list tools and benefits, then miss the deeper effect: a dataset or AI system can define the problem before the official decision begins. By organizing prior studies around negotiation spaces, public discourse, decision outcomes, and human agency, the paper can show the same pattern across fields that otherwise look unrelated. Urban planning and health policy both rely on claims about feasibility; environmental governance and media studies both involve public legitimacy; organizational studies and behavioral science both study how actors respond to mediated choices. The core reason this synthesis is useful is that it follows the movement of evidence through institutions. Data becomes categories, categories become options, options become bargaining positions, and bargaining positions become policy outcomes. That chain explains why the actor with stronger analytical capacity may gain structural power even without formally controlling the final vote.
po: The payoff is a clearer way to ask whether smart city AI is improving public negotiation or quietly narrowing it. The paper gives readers four handles for evaluating the literature: structuring negotiation spaces, shaping discourse and agendas, influencing decisions and negotiated outcomes, and preserving human agency under mediation. That matters for researchers and policy practitioners because it shifts attention from tool accuracy alone to the conditions under which data systems become legitimate, contested, or power-shifting parts of governance. The abstract supports a practical warning: analytical capacity can pre-configure options before deliberation begins.
limits: The abstract describes a work in progress, so the evidence is necessarily partial. It says the review examines highly cited studies from three databases, but it does not show the search terms, inclusion rules, coding procedure, or how disagreements among sources were handled. The provided text also cuts off while discussing algorithmic curation of public information, so the full claim is unavailable here. Because this is a literature review, it can map patterns and tensions, but the abstract does not prove that any specific smart city negotiation was changed by AI in a measured causal way.
